facts.statement: Falcarius was a primitive therizinosaurian theropod dinosaur that lived in North America during the Early Cretaceous period.
facts.quote: Falcarius (meaning "sickle cutter") is a genus of primitive therizinosaurian theropod dinosaurs that lived during the Early Cretaceous period in what is now North America.

facts.statement: Falcarius remains were first collected in the Cedar Mountain Formation in 1999, with more findings occurring in the 2000s.
facts.quote: Its remains were first collected in the Cedar Mountain Formation in 1999, with subsequent findings made during the 2000s.

facts.statement: The genus Falcarius contains two species.
facts.quote: The genus contains two species.

facts.statement: The type species Falcarius utahensis was formally named in 2005.
facts.quote: The type species, Falcarius utahensis, was named in 2005

facts.statement: The species Falcarius suarezarum was originally placed in the distinct genus Geminiraptor in 2010.
facts.quote: The second species, Falcarius suarezarum, was first placed in the distinct genus Geminiraptor in 2010

facts.statement: Falcarius remains were first discovered in 1999 by collector Lawrence Walker at the Crystal Geyser Quarry in Grand County.
facts.quote: The remains of Falcarius were first discovered in 1999 by commercial fossil collector Lawrence Walker at the Crystal Geyser Quarry site in Grand County.

facts.statement: Falcarius was not formally named until a paper was published in the May 2005 issue of the journal Nature.
facts.quote: It was not formally named until a subsequent paper published in the May 2005 issue of the journal Nature.

facts.statement: Falcarius is the most basal known definitive therizinosaurian genus and is considered a transitional form between typical theropods and Therizinosauridae.
facts.quote: Falcarius is the basalmost known definitive therizinosaurian genus, and has been considered a transitional form connecting the typical theropod body plan to the unusual morphology of Therizinosauridae.

facts.statement: The name Falcarius means "sickle cutter" in Latin, referring to the animal's large hand claws.
facts.quote: The generic name, Falcarius, is literally taken from the Latin falcarius (meaning sickle cutter) in reference to the large hand claws.

facts.statement: The smallest Falcarius specimens were under 1 meter long, while average adults reached 4 to 5 meters in length and weighed about 100 kilograms.
facts.quote: While the smallest specimen was approximately less than 1 m, average adults were about 4 - 5 m in length weighing approximately 100 kg.

facts.statement: The skull of Falcarius was small and elongated.
facts.quote: The skull was small and elongated.

facts.statement: Falcarius could reach approximately 1.5 meters off the ground with its long neck to eat leaves or fruit.
facts.quote: With its long neck, Falcarius could apparently reach about 1.5 m off the ground to munch leaves or fruit, possibly higher.

facts.statement: Falcarius had at least sixteen teeth in its upper jaw and twenty-eight teeth in its lower jaw.
facts.quote: The teeth numbered at least sixteen in the maxilla of the upper jaw. The dentary (part of the lower jaw) carried twenty-eight teeth.

facts.statement: Falcarius consumed plant material, as indicated by its small, leaf-shaped, and finely serrated upper teeth.
facts.quote: Its small, leaf-shaped and very finely serrated maxillary teeth indicate that it consumed plant material.

facts.statement: The five longest, straighter, and more pointed teeth in the lower jaw suggest Falcarius might have had a partially omnivorous diet including small animals like lizards.
facts.quote: The front-most five teeth of the lower jaw are much longer, straighter, and more pointed, though, and might indicate a partially omnivorous diet including meat, e.g., small animals such as lizards.

facts.statement: It is debated whether the species Falcarius suarezarum belongs to the troodontid genus Geminiraptor or to the therizinosaur genus Falcarius, as initial identification was based on a single jaw bone before later research suggested it was a therizinosaur similar to F. utahensis.
facts.quote: The second species, Falcarius suarezarum, was first placed in the distinct genus Geminiraptor in 2010 and identified as a troodontid based on a single jaw bone. Later research based on many more fossils from that site indicated the bones instead belong to a therizinosaur very similar to F. utahensis.

facts.statement: A second site known as Suarez Quarry was reported in 2008, containing mainly adult individuals of a perhaps slightly different type.
facts.quote: In 2008, a second site was reported, the Suarez Quarry, with mainly adult individuals, but of a perhaps slightly different type.

facts.statement: By 2010, the number of Falcarius specimens from the original quarry had risen to over 2,700, and later that year exceeded three thousand.
facts.quote: In 2010, the number of specimens from the original quarry had increased to over 2,700, and was later that year reported to have risen to over three thousand.

facts.statement: Two extensive bone beds were discovered containing the remains of hundreds, perhaps thousands, of Falcarius individuals.
facts.quote: Two extensive bone beds were discovered, including the remains of hundreds, perhaps thousands, of individuals of the new species.

facts.statement: In 2010, Geminiraptor suarezarum was described as a new troodontid species based on an isolated maxilla (specimen CEUM 7319) from the Cedar Mountain Formation.
facts.quote: In 2010, Phil Senter and colleagues described Geminiraptor suarezarum as a new genus and species of troodontid based on specimen CEUM 7319, an isolated maxilla recovered from the Lower Yellow Cat Member of the Cedar Mountain Formation.

facts.statement: The holotype specimen of Falcarius, UMNH VP 15000, consists of a partial braincase, with many paratypes assigned.
facts.quote: The holotype specimen, UMNH VP 15000, consists of a partial braincase, and a large number of paratypes were assigned.

facts.statement: Falcarius had a very long neck supported by elongated cervical vertebrae.
facts.quote: The neck was very long with elongated cervical vertebrae.

facts.statement: Falcarius retained a relatively long tail.
facts.quote: The tail was relatively long.

facts.statement: The forelimbs of Falcarius were not particularly long but showed signs of increasing robustness.
facts.quote: The arm as a whole is not especially developed in length but shows signs of increasing robustness.

facts.statement: The exceptionally thick epicondyles of the humerus indicate that Falcarius had strong arm musculature.
facts.quote: The epicondyles are exceptionally thick, indicating a strong musculature.

facts.statement: Falcarius had three toes on its foot that bore weight.
facts.quote: In the foot there were three weight-bearing toes.

facts.statement: The first toe and the first metatarsal of Falcarius did not touch the ground or the ankle.
facts.quote: The first toe did not reach the ground, nor did the first metatarsal touch the ankle.

facts.statement: Falcarius resembles dinosaurs belonging to the Therizinosauridae, a subgroup within Maniraptora.
facts.quote: Falcarius resembles dinosaurs belonging to the Therizinosauridae, part of the group Maniraptora.

facts.statement: Falcarius likely does not belong to Therizinosauridae but is part of the broader group Therizinosauria.
facts.quote: Falcarius itself probably does not belong to this former group, although it does belong to the more inclusive group Therizinosauria.

facts.statement: Therizinosauria is characterized by wider hips, a large braincase, and long necks typical of plant-eaters.
facts.quote: The group is characterized by wider hips, a comparatively large braincase, and long necks typical of plant eaters.

facts.statement: Falcarius shared derived traits with therizinosaurids, including a long neck, a small head with plant-eating teeth, a robust arm with large claws, and a vertical body posture.
facts.quote: Falcarius shared some derived traits with the therizinosaurids: it had a long neck, a small head with teeth adapted for eating plant material, a more robust arm with large hand-claws, and a more vertical position of the body.

facts.statement: It is assumed that Falcarius was covered in quill-like feathers, similar to less basal Asian therizinosaur specimens.
facts.quote: The less basal Asian specimens were covered in quill-like feathers; this is assumed for Falcarius as well.

facts.statement: The genus Falcarius was named by Kirkland and colleagues in 2005.
facts.quote: PBDB name: Falcarius (genus), Kirkland et al. 2005

facts.statement: Falcarius lived during the Berriasian to Valanginian stages, between 143.1 and 132.6 million years ago.
facts.quote: Time range: Berriasian to Valanginian (143.1 to 132.6 million years ago)

facts.statement: Falcarius is considered a transitional form between the original theropod body plan and the more derived Therizinosauridae.
facts.quote: Falcarius can be seen as a transitional form between the original theropod build and the more derived Therizinosauridae.

facts.statement: A 2026 study by Freimuth, Lively, and Zanno reinterpreted the species "Geminiraptor" suarezarum as a member of Therizinosauria belonging to the genus Falcarius.
facts.quote: Freimuth, Lively & Zanno (2026) reinterpret "Geminiraptor" suarezarum as a member of Therizinosauria and as a species belonging to the genus Falcarius.

facts.statement: Smith published a study in 2026 analyzing the biomechanics of the forelimbs of Falcarius.
facts.quote: A study on the biomechanics of the forelimbs of Falcarius is published by Smith (2026).
